item.title: One in four questions in Dutch parliament “written using AI”
item.description:
One in four questions in Dutch parliament “written using AI”

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Around a quarter of questions from MPs in the Dutch parliament were written with the help of AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude, according to research by broadcaster NOS.

NOS analysed 28,000 questions using the AI detection tool Pangram and found that 26% of them showed stylistic features of AI.

Usage peaked at more than 30% just before the summer recess, but dropped to around 17% in July, roughly the same level as a year go.

Some MPs included a sentence or two of AI, while others used to generate whole strings of questions.

Last week prime minister Rob Jetten was criticised after it emerged that around 30% of his social media posts included AI-generated content.

Some of the messages were apparently personal reflections on sensitive subjects such as the mistreatment of Moluccan war veterans in the 1950s, which Jetten recently apologised for on behalf of the government.

Jetten defended the practice, saying that “like three-quarters of Dutch people I sometimes use AI to make things better”.

The use of AI to formulate questions is not necessarily a problem, according to some experts. “If MPs weren’t using it at all I would see that as a bad thing,” AI developer Maarten Sukel told NOS.

But he said it should not be used as a short-cut for in-depth research. “If you’re working on a dossier that you don’t know so much about and you let AI help you come up with questions to ask in parliament, that’s a problem.”

“Faster and smarter”

MP Daniël van den Berg, of the right-wing opposition party JA21, said: “I think it would be a shame for me to spend hours trawling through minutes and documents looking for media items. AI helps me do it faster and smarter.”

But Marleen Stikker, founder of De Digitale Stad, one of the Netherlands’ first online networks, said using AI in parliament undermined Dutch democracy.

“We are outsourcing our democratic system to the American AI companies’ algorithms, which aren’t even neutral, they’re skewed. That’s absurd, surely?”

item.title: Children in Dutch care system exploited on placements abroad
item.description:
Children in Dutch care system exploited on placements abroad

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Children in the Dutch care system may be being exploited while on youth placements abroad, an investigation by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur has found.

Councils and child protection agencies can sometimes send children with behavioural problems to other countries, such as Spain, when there is no suitable place for them in the Netherlands. This is supposed to be a temporary solution but some end up staying for up to three years.

The investigation found that the health and youth care inspectorate (IGJ) has been flagging risks in the system since 2009, but parliament was never informed. The inspectorate now says it is receiving reports of children being forced into unpaid work, locked up and not going to school, and admits that nothing has changed.

Because the IGJ has no jurisdiction in foreign countries it cannot investigate reports itself. Some children are also being sent outside the EU, the investigation found, some to Morocco.

Those placed in Morocco have no background in the country, which the organisation running the site, Multi Plus Zorg, said is an advantage because it makes the children more dependent on staff and lets them focus on their own development. Youth law professor Mariëlle Bruning told the programme it “smells of abuse”.

The IGJ said “peer pressure” was being used in some places to keep children under control, and that some were subjected to “outdated” methods focused on punishment.

It also said it has reports of children being physically restrained and barred from leaving the grounds, neither of which is permitted in this type of care, and of some having to do heavy work instead of going to school.

The inspectorate last counted how many Dutch children were in care abroad in 2007, when there were 330.

Youth care minister Mirjam Sterk said she found the situation “worrying”. Parliament passed a motion earlier this year to limit placements abroad as far as possible.

item.title: Croatian couple on run from Slovenia arrested near Dutch border
item.description:
Croatian couple on run from Slovenia arrested near Dutch border

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Croatian couple who went into hiding in the Netherlands after being sought in connection with a murder in Slovenia have been arrested across the border in Germany.

The 31-year-old man and 29-year-old woman were stopped in Isterberg, near the border town of Nordhorn, by plainclothes police officers on Friday evening.

Police believe they had just crossed the border from the Netherlands because strict checks are in place on the German side.

Slovenian prosecutors had issued a European arrest warrant for the couple, who are suspected of torture, strangulation and murder.

German police took them into custody in Oldenburg, where they appeared in court on Saturday for an extradition hearing. Their car was also confiscated.

The Telegraaf reported that the couple had been living in the Netherlands and driving in a car with false registration plates. The man did not have a valid driving licence.

item.title: Three Dutch die in small airplane crash in Germany
item.description:
Three Dutch die in small airplane crash in Germany

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A small aircraft carrying three Dutch people crashed in Erkelenz, not far from the German border near Roermand. Local police confirmed all three were dead at the scene on Monday morning.

The victims were a 57-year-old man from the Súdwest-Fryslân area of Friesland, and a 58-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman, both from Amsterdam, the foreign affairs ministry told broadcaster NOS. Their names have not been released but next of kin have been notified, the ministry said.

The plane, a four-seat Cessna 172, belonged to Vliegschool Hilversum, a flight school based at the airfield outside Hilversum. Flight tracking data show it took off at 10.25am and disappeared from radar at 11.18am near Erkelenz.

The school released a statement: “With great concern we announce that an accident has occurred in Germany involving one of our aircraft, a Cessna 172. The circumstances of the incident are still unclear.”

The school has halted all its flights while the investigation into the crash is ongoing. The purpose of the flight, and what caused it to crash, has not been made clear.

Dutch aviation safety investigators are joining German authorities to establish what happened, broadcaster NOS reported.

German media reports indicate that the plane may have been on route to Freiburg, and that the pilot had contacted air traffic control due to bad weather before the plane began losing altitude and crashed.

item.title: Far-right party school research was misleading, experts say
item.description:
Far-right party school research was misleading, experts say

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The research which led the government to put €507,000 into a primary school backed by far-right party Forum voor Democratie was flawed and did not include key information, experts have told the Volkskrant.

The Renaissance school opened its doors in Almere this school year with just four pupils, well below the number required for official funding. But officials agreed to back the school because research apparently showed there would be a demand for new schools in the area over the coming years.

However, Peter Kanne from market research bureau Ipsos I&O told the Volkskrant that the questionnaire did not tell prospective parents the school was allied to the party and instead asked general questions about their thoughts on education.

Some 35,000 invitations to take part in the research were sent to the homes in the Almere Oosterwold area – which is several kilometres from the school’s location.

In total 258 parents responded and 18 parents said they would like their child to attend the school, the Volkskrant said, after using freedom of information legislation.

That percentage is extremely low, making it impossible to determine if the research was representative, professor Tom Louwerse told the paper. “This research says little or nothing about the potential of the school,” he said.

Experts also criticised the questioning, in which parents were asked to choose options such as “a focus on reading and arithmetic” and “lessons five days a week” – which all Dutch schools offer. Nor did the survey mention that girls and boys will be taught differently.

The education ministry said in response to MPs’ questions earlier that all the rules for the research had been followed.

D66 parliamentarian Ilana Rooderkerk told the paper the school was launched “under false pretences” and has submitted a string of questions to the minister. “We need to ditch this sort of misleading research,” she said. “Children should never become the subject of a political project.”

An earlier attempt to open a Renaissance school in Almere, which was fully funded by parents and private sources, failed and closed in 2024.

item.title: Unrest in Rotterdam after man dies in mistaken arrest
item.description:
Unrest in Rotterdam after man dies in mistaken arrest

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The death of a Rotterdam man who was arrested by police on Saturday for purportedly riding a stolen fatbike has sparked unrest in the city after it turned out he was not who they were looking for. Police confirmed that his fatbike was the wrong one, and prosecutors said he resisted arrest and then died shortly afterwards despite their attempts to resuscitate him.

The 51-year old, Alfredo Goeloe, was out to collect diabetes medication, according to his family, when police approached as they were searching for a stolen fatbike.

He failed to produce identification, public prosecutors said, and ran from them. Once they caught him he tried to escape their restraints and then fell immediately unwell.

Some of the events were caught on camera, including him screaming in pain and shouting that he had diabetes as additional police rushed to assist the arrest.

A 45-second video of the event, which cut off before he fell ill, was taken by a passer by. The footage is being investigated and Goeloe’s relatives are being assisted by an organisation called Controle Alt Delete, which works against ethnic profiling.

His family’s lawyer also told the talk show Pauw en de Wit on Monday night that they will file a criminal complaint. Goeloe’s partner is expecting a child.

A silent march in Rotterdam was held last night in tribute to Goeloe, which proceeded peacefully but ended with some unrest outside the Zuidplein police station, where riot police formed a line in front of the marchers and fireworks were thrown. One person was arrested.

item.title: Olympic champion Jutta Leerdam hangs up her skates, for now
item.description:
Olympic champion Jutta Leerdam hangs up her skates, for now

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Olympic speed skating champion Jutta Leerdam will not take part in any competitions in the coming season, but says she is not ditching the sport altogether.

The 27-year-old, who won gold in the 1,000 metres and silver in the 500 metres at the winter games in Milan, said at the time she had doubts about her future. Now she has confirmed a season break, saying on her YouTube channel, “I am following my feelings”.

“Am I retiring? One thing is sure. You will not see me skate this season. I won’t be competing this year. You won’t see me on the ice.”

Leerdam, who is engaged to marry American social media star Jake Paul, said she was not closing the door on skating for good. “Retirement feels very final,” she said. “It would feel like closing the door on something I really love.”

Leerdam, who now lives in the US, said she plans to focus more on making videos for social media – she has 6.3 million followers on Instagram – and other “cool projects”.

In the post, Leerdam talks about the pressure of winning and her personal drive to become Olympic champion. “What feels right, right now, is choosing me,” she said in the 11-minute video.

Other Dutch skating champions say they are sorry Leerdam will not be taking part in this season’s competitions, in which Dutch women sprinters have a leading role.

But former champion turned analyst Mark Tuitert said he expected to see her back. “The Olympics take place in the Netherlands in four years’ time,” he told broadcaster NOS. “So the door has not been shut completely… she would be 31 then, and I think she can do it.”

item.title: Minister pledges to end secrecy on property foundation reports
item.description:
Minister pledges to end secrecy on property foundation reports

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan has pledged to make information about property foundations accessible to home owners from next year, ending the current secrecy.

At the moment the information, which is a key part of getting a mortgage, can only be accessed by estate agents and banks.

Since April 1 a simple foundations check has become part of the big banks’ mortgage requirements but this is only done once buyers have made an offer. Foundations are graded A to E, with D and E labels requiring further research. Buyers whose potential property scores D or E could end up being denied a mortgage because of the cost of repairs.

The minister told consumer rights show Radar on Monday night that home owners had the right to know everything officials know about their property.

She said “all available and verified information” about the foundations of their property will now be included in a new section on the MijnOverheid website – a government-run digital information hub.

“People who are looking for a house should know what the foundations label is, as they do with an energy label,” the minister said. The new section will come online next year but it will take until 2030 for all the information to be included.

A survey of 750 members of Radar’s viewers panel showed that most buyers – 86% – do not make a foundations check a condition of making an offer on a house.

But if banks discover the foundations are faulty, they could end up denying the buyer a mortgage – leaving them with costs to pay for defaulting on an offer.

Thousands of buildings

Government advisory group RLI said in July that more than 400,000 buildings in the Netherlands have problems with their foundations or are likely to develop them in the next 10 years.

Buildings are sinking for a combination of reasons, including falling groundwater levels, bacterial erosion, drought, structural faults and the impact of construction work.

In around 120,000 cases the buildings are in urgent need of repair, the council said, and if nothing is done the cost of repairing the damage could add up to €54 billion.

Six in 10 home owners whose property needs urgent repairs to the foundations cannot afford to pay for them, financial services authority AFM said in April.

item.title: Prinsjesdag: what you need to know about the rituals
item.description:
Prinsjesdag: what you need to know about the rituals

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The government presents its 2027 spending plans to parliament and the public on Tuesday. Here’s what you need to know:

Prinsjesdag, the day the king opens the new parliamentary year and the government publishes its plans, has taken place on the third Tuesday in September since 1887.

The day’s events kick off at 1pm when king Willem-Alexander and queen Máxima travel from Noordeinde palace to the Koninklijke Schouwburg theatre in a horse-drawn coach, accompanied by princess Amalia, who has ridden with her parents every year since her Prinsjesdag debut in 2022.

The coach is the Glass Coach, which was delivered to King Willem I in 1826 and marks its 200th anniversary this year. It has been used since 2016, when the Golden Coach, with its side panels depicting black slaves submitting to a white woman, was taken away for restoration. That work was completed in 2021, but the king said in 2022 that the Golden Coach would not be used again until society is ready and it has not been seen on Prinsjesdag since.

At the theatre the king will address the members of the upper and lower houses of parliament, plus the diplomatic corps, and outline the government’s plans for the coming year. Reading out the troonrede (speech from the throne), which is written by the government, is one of the monarch’s main ceremonial jobs.

The speech is traditionally given in the splendour of the Ridderzaal, or knights’ hall, on the Binnenhof, but this is the fifth year running it takes place at the theatre because the parliamentary complex is undergoing major renovations.

Nevertheless, the hats worn by female guests – the hoedjesparade – are likely to provide much fodder for the gossip columns, as they do every year.

After the speech, the royals will return to the palace by coach and appear on the balcony with other members of the family to wave at the crowds at around 2pm.

At 3pm, finance minister Eelco Heinen will present the budget, or rijksbegroting, to parliament. The paperwork is always delivered in the same briefcase, a tradition which started in 1947, although the current goatskin case has only been in service since 1964. It is Heinen’s third budget but the first for the Jetten cabinet, the minority coalition of D66, the VVD and the CDA which was sworn in in February.

The rijksbegroting literally means state budget and sets out how much money each ministry has been allocated for the coming calendar year and what the spending priorities are. A close cousin to the rijksbegroting is the miljoenennota, which is the breakdown of the finances, outlining the economic and financial situation in the country.

A third document is the annual macro economische verkenning (MEV) or macro-economic outlook, which is drawn up by the government’s economic policy advisory agency CPB. It contains all the forecasts which ministers have used to work out their spending plans and calculates what the effect of those policies is likely to be.

Leaks
Another Prinsjesdag tradition is the way much of the budget is leaked to the media in advance, and 2026 is no exception. Details reported by the Dutch press so far include a marginal fall in spending power for everyone except pensioners and low-income households, a delay until 2029 in cutting unemployment benefit from two years to one, a scrapped €60 increase in the health insurance own risk payment, extra money for education, housing and defence, and a €100 to €300 sport pass for 12 to 23-year-olds.

Debates
On the Wednesday and Thursday after the formal presentation of the budget, MPs debate the main socio-economic points with the prime minister and finance minister in the Algemene Politieke Beschouwingen, which is seen as the most important parliamentary debate of the year. It will be prime minister Rob Jetten’s first as head of government.

Opposition leaders will come up with their own alternative budgets and argue for changes to the government plans. The government always agrees to include some of their measures.

In the following weeks, each ministry’s spending plans will come under the spotlight in a two-day debate with each individual minister in the hot seat.

Legislation
As the debates progress, legislation based on the plans will be drawn up and voted on – and often little remains of the original idea. This year the changes are likely to be particularly strong, given that the coalition is short of a majority in the lower house and in the senate, and its attempt to agree a package with opposition parties before Prinsjesdag collapsed. Jetten himself has said the budget presented on Tuesday is “not the end”.

There is also usually a rush to get key changes to the law signed and sealed before the end of the year.

DutchNews will publish a summary of the king’s speech and a round-up of the government’s main plans on Tuesday afternoon.

item.title: Dutch railway network disrupted by sabotage to tracks
item.description:
Dutch railway network disrupted by sabotage to tracks

September 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Train services across the Netherlands were disrupted on Tuesday morning in what network operators say was an act of co-ordinated sabotage.

ProRail, the company responsible for managing the track network, said security systems had been disrupted in 24 places, making it impossible for trains to run.

Railway workers found sections of pipe attached to the rails when they inspected the tracks at 5.30am. A train collided with one of the sections at Steenwijk, but no injuries were reported, ProRail said.

Spokeswoman Joke van der Cruysen told NOS there was clear evidence of sabotage and ProRail expects to find more sites during the course of the day.

“We have been to these places and carried out investigations and found materials that were intentionally put there,” she said. “So we can say the railway has been sabotaged.”

“Our priority is to make sure these materials are removed from the railway, the evidence is secured and we can restart train services as quickly as possible.”

AIVD investigating

The national intelligence agency AIVD said it was working with police to try to identify “which direction this comes from”. However, the national anti-terrorism co-ordinator would not comment on whether the saboteurs had a terrorist motive.

Junior transport minister Annet Bertram said it was “extremely concerning” that the trains had been deliberately tampered with. “This needs to be investigated thoroughly,” she said.

The biggest delays are to services north of Utrecht, but train operator NOS said the disruption would affect the entire country. NS hopes to start running trains through Amersfoort, Zwolle and Deventer again after midday.

ProRail said pieces of pipe were attached to the rails, triggering the safety mechanisms that monitor whether trains are on the track and causing signals to turn red.

Steel pipes measuring up to 2 metres long were found in at least five locations in Gelderland.

The Reisplanner app used by travellers to plan their journey was also out of service during the morning rush-hour.

NS has advised people to check the app before setting out on their journey. No replacement buses have been arranged because the disruption is too widespread, a spokesman said.

Opening of parliament

The chaos is also expected to spread to the roads because the barriers at some level crossings are permanently down due to the problems with the security systems.

A ProRail spokesman said: “Our colleagues are working hard to clear these materials and make the situation safe. Where possible we will resume train services as quickly as possible. We are also in close contact with emergency services and other relevant parties.”

Media speculated that the sabotage could have been timed to coincide with Prinsjesdag, the state opening of parliament in The Hague and one of the biggest days in the Dutch political calendar.

Thousands of people travel across the country to watch king Willem-Alexander travel through the streets in a horse-drawn carriage before delivering his annual speech setting out the government’s legislative programme for the year.

One royal fan hoping to travel from Apeldoorn told Omroep Gelderland: “We looked at the big board and I thought: ‘uh-oh’. Then my sister looked at the app and saw that there were no trains until 8.30.”
